title: The Gueuloir and the Nile: Croisset, Egypt, and the Sentence Ground Down
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Hotel-Dieu and the College Royal

stops.name: Hotel-Dieu de Rouen, the birth in the surgeon's apartment
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinate corrected to 51 rue de Lecat (Musee Flaubert et d'histoire de la medecine), not the Rouen city-centre pin carried by two of the research lenses
stops.campa: Achille-Cleophas Flaubert is chief surgeon of the Hotel-Dieu of Rouen, and the apartment on the first floor comes with the post. His second son is born there on the twelfth of December, inside a working hospital. The dissecting room is across the courtyard, and the boy and his sister Caroline climb the garden wall to look at the cadavers laid out under flies. He is raised in the smell of a ward and the vocabulary of a man who cuts. Thirty years later he will write a clubfoot operation and a death by arsenic in the flat tone the household kept for such things.
sources: Wikipedia FR, 'Musee Flaubert et d'histoire de la medecine'
suggested_refs: The surgeon's apartment on the first floor of the Hotel-Dieu, now the Musee Flaubert et d'histoire de la medecine

stops.name: College royal de Rouen, the boarder and the expulsion
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia FR chronology); month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He enters the College royal of Rouen as a boarder at ten and stays seven years. With Ernest Chevalier he founds a manuscript journal, Art et Progres, and copies out plays and histories in a hand already impatient with them. In December 1839 the school expels him for indiscipline, months short of his examinations, and he takes the baccalaureat the following year as an external candidate. The building is renamed for Pierre Corneille in April 1873, when the expelled pupil is the most exacting novelist in France and has not set foot in it since.
suggested_refs: Art et Progres, the manuscript school journal of 1834
The register of the College royal recording the December 1839 expulsion

stops.name: Trouville-sur-Mer, Elisa Schlesinger on the sand
stops.date_confidence: year attested, August traditional; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: On the beach at Trouville a fourteen-year-old sees Elisa Schlesinger, wife of a Paris music publisher and eleven years older than he is. The tradition has him carrying her cloak up out of the tide line; the chronologies record only the meeting. Nothing follows from it. He sees her at intervals for the rest of his life and never has her, and she goes on arriving in the fiction under other names, most completely as Madame Arnoux in L'Education sentimentale, a woman the hero adores for thirty years and touches twice.
suggested_refs: The Trouville strand of 1836, and Madame Arnoux in L'Education sentimentale (1869)

segments.name: The Journey South and the Abandoned Law

stops.name: Bagneres-de-Luchon, the reward journey
stops.date_confidence: year attested; August traditional, day defaulted to 01. The research pool's single Pyrenees-Corsica midpoint (42.6, 1.0) was a meaningless coordinate and is split here into Luchon and Ajaccio
stops.campa: The baccalaureat won, his parents pay for a journey south. He travels in the company of the family friend Doctor Jules Cloquet rather than with his mother and father, and the itinerary runs through the Pyrenean spa towns, Luchon among them, taken as much for the boy's nervous constitution as for the scenery. He is eighteen and writing everything down, already keeping the traveller's notebook that will follow him to the Nile. The mountains do not move him much. What he records is inns, prices, faces, the weather, and what people say at table.
sources: Standard biography: Flaubert travels with Jules Cloquet, parents funding
suggested_refs: Flaubert's 1840 travel notes, Pyrenees et Corse

stops.name: Ajaccio, Corsica and the return by Marseille
stops.date_confidence: year attested; September inferred from the itinerary, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The journey carries him across to Corsica and he lands at Ajaccio, Napoleon's birth town, four decades after the Egyptian campaign that taught France to want the Orient. He rides the interior, notes the bandits and the maquis, and turns for home by way of Marseille, where at the Hotel Richelieu he meets Eulalie Foucaud de Langlade and has the first affair of his life. The Corsican leg gives him a taste for hot countries. The Marseille night gives him something he prefers not to name in front of his mother, and remembers for nine years.
sources: Standard biographical account of the Eulalie Foucaud episode at Marseille
suggested_refs: The Hotel Richelieu, Marseille, and the Eulalie Foucaud correspondence

stops.name: Sorbonne quarter, Paris, law without conviction
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He is sent to Paris to read law and does it badly on purpose. Lectures near the Sorbonne, lodgings, a code memorized and hated, an examination failed: three years pass in a discipline he never intends to finish. He prefers the salons, the sculptor Pradier's studio, and the company of men who write. What Paris supplies is not a profession but the raw stock of L'Education sentimentale, the boarding houses and student politics and cafe talk of the 1840s, set down twenty-five years later by a man who was bored at the time and forgot nothing.
suggested_refs: The Paris law faculty registers, 1841-1844

stops.name: The road near Pont-l'Eveque, the first seizure
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION UNRESOLVED: Wikipedia FR dates the first seizure January 1844, Wikipedia EN gives 1846. The French date is used here; the English one is not thereby refuted. Day defaulted to 01, coordinate approximate for the Pont-l'Eveque road
stops.campa: Driving at night on a road near Pont-l'Eveque with his brother Achille, he is thrown down by a seizure and lies in the cart believing himself dead. The French chronology dates it January 1844; English Wikipedia gives 1846, and the two are left standing here. Whatever the year, the effect is exact. The law is abandoned with a doctor's authority, and the family accepts that this son will not have a profession. The illness that ruins his twenties buys him the only thing he wants, which is a room and the whole of his own time.
suggested_refs: The Flaubert family medical correspondence on the 1844 crisis

stops.name: Croisset, the house on the Seine
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; day defaulted to 01. Coordinate is the Pavillon Flaubert at 18 quai Gustave-Flaubert, Canteleu; two of the three research lenses carried Croisset pins roughly two kilometres wrong
stops.campa: His father buys a long white house at Croisset on the Seine below Rouen, and the family moves in in June. Flaubert is twenty-two and lives here thirty-five years. From the study he watches the river traffic going down to Le Havre. He writes standing at a desk, shouts sentences aloud in the gueuloir to test what they do to a voice, and works through nights that end at four. Madame Bovary, Salammbo, L'Education sentimentale, Trois Contes, and the unfinished Bouvard et Pecuchet are all made in this one room. Everything else in the life is a departure from it.
stops.quote: Be regular and orderly in your life like a bourgeois, so that you may be violent and original in your work.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to a letter to Gertrude Tennant, 1876; widely quoted (Wikiquote) but not verified in a fetched primary edition
suggested_refs: The Pavillon Flaubert, sole surviving fragment of the Croisset property

stops.name: Rouen, the surgeon dies and the sister after him
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia FR chronology); month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Achille-Cleophas dies early in the year and Caroline, the sister, dies within weeks of puerperal fever after childbirth. Flaubert has her face cast in plaster and keeps the mask. In a single winter the household that raised him is reduced to himself, his mother, and an infant niece he will father as well as he can. He also inherits, and the surgeon's money is what pays for Egypt three years later. In the letters of this year he sets down his own grief the way the surgeon set down a case.
stops.quote: Each one of us carries within himself his necropolis.
stops.quote_source: The George Sand-Gustave Flaubert Letters, Letter XXVI, Flaubert to Sand, Monday night, 1866, Project Gutenberg ebook #5115
suggested_refs: The plaster death mask of Caroline Flaubert, kept at Croisset

segments.name: Louise Colet and the Breton Roads

stops.name: Atelier Pradier, Paris, the meeting with Louise Colet
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia FR, 'Louise Colet': the meeting takes place in Pradier's studio in 1846); month and day inferred, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In the studio of the sculptor James Pradier he is introduced to Louise Colet, poet, salonniere, eleven years his senior and already famous for her temper. The liaison runs nine years, from the spring of 1846 to the sixth of March 1855, in two stages and mostly on paper. Some accounts round it down to eight; the chronology gives 1846 to 1855. He refuses to let her come to Croisset. What she gets instead is the greatest working correspondence in French literature, hundreds of letters in which he takes his own sentences apart in front of her.
suggested_refs: The Flaubert-Colet correspondence, 1846-1855

stops.name: Mont Saint-Michel, the abbey on the tide
stops.date_confidence: the Brittany tour with Du Camp begins in May 1847 and runs three months; the Mont Saint-Michel leg is placed in June by itinerary, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He walks Brittany with Maxime Du Camp for three months in 1847, on foot and by carriage, and climbs to the abbey on its rock in the bay. The two men write the trip up in alternating chapters, Flaubert taking the odd ones: Par les champs et par les greves. Du Camp's sections appear in the Revue de Paris from April 1852; Flaubert's own wait until Charpentier prints them on the fifteenth of October 1881, a year after he is dead. It is his apprenticeship in the traveller's notebook.
sources: Wikipedia FR, 'Par les champs et par les greves'
suggested_refs: Par les champs et par les greves, Flaubert's chapters, Charpentier, 15 October 1881

stops.name: Mantes-la-Jolie, the halfway room
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No document in the reachable sources fixes a dated meeting at Mantes; the town is the standard biographical account of the couple's rendezvous point, and the date here is a placeholder inside the 1846-1854 span
stops.campa: Mantes sits midway between Paris and Rouen, and the biographical tradition puts the meetings here: a hired room, a train each way, the affair conducted at the exact geographic compromise between her demand and his refusal. Nothing in the reachable sources fixes a specific dated night in the town, so the pin is a reconstruction from the correspondence. The shape of the arrangement is not in doubt. He will not live with her, he will not stop writing to her, and he does his loving at a distance measured in kilometres and postage.
stops.quote: An author in his book must be like God in the universe, present everywhere and visible nowhere.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to a letter to Louise Colet, 9 December 1852; widely cited (Wikiquote) but not verified in a primary correspondence volume. The primary-source formulation is in the 1875 Sand letter used below
sources: Francis Steegmuller, Flaubert and Madame Bovary
suggested_refs: The Flaubert-Colet meeting places between Paris and Rouen

stops.name: Croisset, the Temptation read aloud for four days
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested (Wikipedia EN); day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He finishes the first Tentation de saint Antoine and summons Louis Bouilhet and Du Camp to Croisset. Over four days he reads them the whole of it aloud, hours of desert hallucination. Their verdict at the end: throw it in the fire, never speak of it again, take an ordinary subject, a provincial story, something small. He obeys and does not obey. The hermit of the Thebaid, Anthony the Great, whose desert lay near Coma in Middle Egypt, will be rewritten twice more and published at last in 1874.
suggested_refs: The 1849 manuscript of La Tentation de saint Antoine, first version

stops.name: Croisset, the departure of 22 October
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia FR, 'Voyage en Egypte'). The research pool mismatched this date to Marseille; the Croisset departure is 22 October, the Marseille sailing 4 November
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of October he leaves Croisset with Du Camp for a journey east that will last a year and a half. Du Camp carries an archaeological mission from the Ministere de l'Instruction publique and a camera. Flaubert carries a commission of his own, obtained for form's sake and never executed, and the surgeon's inheritance. His mother comes to the gate. He is twenty-seven, has published nothing, and has just been told by his two closest friends that his masterpiece is unreadable. He goes to Egypt instead of arguing with them.
suggested_refs: Du Camp's ministerial mission archeologique, 1849

stops.name: Vieux-Port, Marseille, aboard Le Nil
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia FR, 'Voyage en Egypte')
stops.campa: They sail from the Vieux-Port on the fourth of November aboard the steamer Le Nil, bound for Alexandria by the Malta packet route. Nine years earlier he passed through this city as a schoolboy and spent a night at the Hotel Richelieu; he goes to look at the building and finds it turned into a bazaar. He arrives everywhere slightly too late, writes down what is actually in front of him rather than what was supposed to be there, and keeps both versions on the page.
suggested_refs: The steamer Le Nil and the Marseille-Alexandria packet line of 1849

stops.name: Alexandria, the landfall
stops.date_confidence: mid-November attested; the exact day is the standard biographical date and is not independently confirmed here. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the atlas Alexandria pin used by ibn_battuta, abdelkader, and san_antonio_abad
stops.campa: He comes ashore at Alexandria in the middle of November, his first ground outside Europe. He rides inland to the Roman column called Pompey's Pillar, which stands not over the water but in the ruined temenos of the Serapeum, and opens the notebook he has kept since the Pyrenees journey of 1840, filling it now with a country he has wanted to see since boyhood. The letters he sends home from here already carry the flat, exact notation Bouilhet will get more of from Cairo onward.
suggested_refs: Pompey's Pillar and the Serapeum temenos, Alexandria
Du Camp's Alexandria calotypes, 1849

stops.name: Giza, the Sphinx and the business card
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested from the correspondence; day defaulted to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the atlas Giza pin used by gurdjieff
stops.campa: He rides out to the plateau in December and the Sphinx looks back at him, terrifyingly, as he puts it in the notes. He climbs the Great Pyramid before dawn and finds nailed at the summit the business card of a wallpaper manufacturer from Rouen: a Norman tradesman's advertisement planted on the oldest monument he has ever stood on. Du Camp sets up the camera below and makes some of the earliest photographs of the monuments taken by anyone, and the plateau does to the pair of them what it does to every traveller, which is refuse to be adequately described.
sources: Francis Steegmuller, Flaubert in Egypt: A Sensibility on Tour
suggested_refs: The Rouen wallpaper manufacturer's card at the summit of the Great Pyramid

stops.name: Cairo, the Ezbekieh nights
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested from the Bouilhet letters; day defaulted to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the atlas Cairo pin used by blavatsky
stops.campa: He spends the winter in Cairo: mosques, bathhouses, bazaars, the Muhammad Ali mosque on the citadel still an open building site eighteen years into a construction that will not be finished until 1857. In the Ezbekieh quarter he visits the houses of the dancers and the prostitutes and writes it all to Bouilhet in Rouen with a clinical frankness that has embarrassed editors ever since. It is the same notebook habit that will carry him, within weeks, up the Nile to Esna and the room he describes in no less exact a hand.
sources: Flaubert's letters to Louis Bouilhet, January 1850, in Steegmuller, Flaubert in Egypt
suggested_refs: The Ezbekieh quarter of Cairo in 1850
The Mosque of Muhammad Ali under construction, 1832-1857

stops.name: Esna, the night with Kuchuk Hanem
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the Voyage en Egypte notebooks
stops.campa: Sailing upriver they stop at Esna, where the dancers expelled from Cairo have been resettled. Flaubert spends an evening and a night with Kuchuk Hanem, courtesan and almeh, and records the room, the bedbugs, her necklace, her breathing while she sleeps, and his own thoughts while she does. It is the most exact page he writes in Egypt and the one most used against him. She becomes the pattern for every eastern woman in his fiction and never speaks in any of it, which is the whole of the charge and also, he would say, the method.
stops.quote: I maintain that cynicism borders on chastity.
stops.quote_source: The George Sand-Gustave Flaubert Letters, Letter XVII, Flaubert to Sand, Croisset, 1866, Project Gutenberg ebook #5115
suggested_refs: The Kuchuk Hanem pages of the Voyage en Egypte, 6 March 1850

stops.name: Karnak, the hypostyle hall
stops.date_confidence: March 1850 attested; the day is reconstructed from the upstream itinerary after the 6 March Esna stop
stops.campa: At Karnak he walks the hypostyle hall of Amun, a forest of columns holding up nothing, and finds he cannot write about it without falling into the phrases every traveller before him has used. He notes that difficulty instead of solving it. Du Camp photographs the columns on the same visit, among the earliest images ever made of the site, and pays his hired Nubian to stand at their bases so the plate will carry a scale. Between the two of them the record is complete: one man measuring the stone, the other admitting it defeats him.
suggested_refs: Du Camp, Egypte, Nubie, Palestine et Syrie (1852), the Karnak plates

stops.name: Philae, the island temple of Isis
stops.date_confidence: CORRECTION: the research pool dated Philae February 1850, which is internally impossible, since Philae lies far upriver of Esna and the Esna stop is dated 6 March. Placed here in mid-March by itinerary; the day is reconstructed. Coordinate is the temple on Agilkia, where it now stands
stops.campa: Above Aswan the boat reaches Philae and the temple of Isis on its island, the last place in Egypt where the old gods were served, four centuries after Rome turned Christian. He counts it among the affecting sights of the journey. The island he sees is the original one. The Aswan dams will drown it, and between 1977 and 1979 the whole temple is cut apart and rebuilt on higher ground at Agilkia, where the coordinate now sits. He is looking at a place that has since been physically moved out from under his description of it.
suggested_refs: The Philae relocation to Agilkia, 1977-1979

stops.name: Abu Simbel, the colossi and the hired Nubian
stops.date_confidence: March 1850 attested for Du Camp's photograph; the day is reconstructed from the itinerary
stops.campa: The boat carries them into Nubia to Abu Simbel, where four seated Ramesses face the river out of the cliff with the sand still banked to their chests. Du Camp makes the photograph that outlives them both, standing his hired Nubian, Hadji-Ishmael, against a colossus for scale. They go on upstream to Wadi Halfa and the Second Cataract before turning, so Abu Simbel is near the far point of the journey and not the far point itself. He is nearly as far from Rouen as he will ever be.
suggested_refs: Du Camp's Abu Simbel plate with Hadji-Ishmael, March 1850

segments.name: The Levant and the Long Way Home

stops.name: Beirut, the harbour and the infection
stops.date_confidence: year attested, July from the French chronology; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: They leave Egypt by sea and land at Beirut in July. Here, by the French chronology, he contracts syphilis, one of several venereal infections picked up on the journey. His hair begins to fall out within the year and the mercury treatment does the rest of the damage. He is twenty-eight. The disease runs under the whole of the remaining life alongside the seizures, and he keeps it out of the fiction entirely. What goes into the fiction from this coast is the Carthage of Salammbo and the Judaea of Herodias, both built from books.
suggested_refs: The Beirut leg of the Voyage en Orient, July 1850

stops.name: Jerusalem, the sanctuaries walked without belief
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested from the itinerary; day defaulted to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the atlas Temple Mount pin used by ibn_battuta
stops.campa: He tours Jerusalem in August, the Holy Sepulchre among the stations, and finds the sacred city interesting as spectacle and repellent as devotion: rival clergy, oil lamps, the smell of the crowd. Ibn Battuta crossed this same esplanade in 1326 and called it the third sanctuary, in passing. Flaubert takes notes toward a Herodias he will not write for twenty-seven years. The pilgrim route makes a serviceable itinerary for a man with no faith left, because everything on it is already famous and can therefore be checked against the thing itself.
sources: Francis Steegmuller, Flaubert in Egypt (Levant chapters)
suggested_refs: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in 1850, and Herodias (1877)

stops.name: Damascus, the Umayyad Mosque
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Syria is on the itinerary but no reachable source puts Flaubert inside the Umayyad Mosque on a named day; date and day are inferred. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the atlas Umayyad Mosque pin used by abdelkader
stops.campa: The Levantine leg carries them inland to Damascus and the great Umayyad Mosque, its courtyard the size of a parade ground, raised on the site of a Roman temple that had already been a Byzantine church before it became a mosque. Flaubert walks the courtyard among worshippers and idlers and takes down what he sees without commentary, in the same clinical hand he used in Cairo. Within the week they turn back toward the coast and Rhodes; the Levant leg of the journey is nearly over.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque courtyard, Damascus

stops.name: Rhodes, the Old Town
stops.date_confidence: Rhodes attested on the itinerary (Wikipedia FR); month inferred, day defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected to the medieval town, the research pool's pin sitting 1.3 km southwest in the modern city
stops.campa: Sailing north for Constantinople they put in at Rhodes, and he walks the crusader town the Knights Hospitaller built and lost, the Street of the Knights running up to the palace of the Grand Master. The journey has turned into a survey of empires that finished: pharaonic, Roman, Byzantine, Frankish, Ottoman, each laid over the last on the same rock. He is composing nothing yet. He is loading a memory that will supply Carthage in eight years and the Thebaid in twenty-four, both of them cities he never saw standing.
suggested_refs: The Street of the Knights and the Palace of the Grand Master, Rhodes

stops.name: Hagia Sophia, Constantinople, five weeks
stops.date_confidence: five weeks in Constantinople attested (Wikipedia); month placed by itinerary, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Five weeks in Constantinople, and by the end of them he is tired of monuments. He walks Hagia Sophia, the mosques of the old city, the cemeteries and the dog packs, and complains in his letters home of sightseeing as a form of labour. He also sends Bouilhet a list of books he might make, three subjects turned over like stones, one of them a provincial story. Greece and Italy follow, and he is back at Croisset by June 1851, nineteen months away and nothing decided on paper. Sources disagree on the return date; the French chronology is followed here.
suggested_refs: The Constantinople letters to Louis Bouilhet, November 1850

stops.name: Croisset, the first page of Madame Bovary
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia FR chronology)
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of September he sits down and begins. It takes fifty-six months. He writes standing, at a rate that sometimes runs to a page a week, hunting assonance out of every sentence and reading each one aloud in the gueuloir until it survives the voice. Louise Colet gets the bulletins: seven hours for a paragraph, a day lost to a comma, the agricultural show taking three months. The subject is the one Bouilhet and Du Camp prescribed as a cure for his imagination, a doctor's wife in a Norman market town with nothing whatever to her.
stops.quote: We were in class when the head-master came in, followed by a 'new fellow,' not wearing the school uniform, and a school servant carrying a large desk.
stops.quote_source: Madame Bovary, Part I, Chapter I, trans. Eleanor Marx-Aveling, Project Gutenberg ebook #2413
suggested_refs: The Madame Bovary manuscript drafts, Bibliotheque municipale de Rouen

stops.name: Paris, the end of Louise Colet
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia FR chronology)
stops.campa: On the sixth of March 1855 it ends, definitively, after nine years. She comes to his door and is turned away, and the last note he writes her tells her not to come again. She will publish a novel with a portrait of him in it, drawn from the inside and not kindly. He keeps every one of her letters. The correspondence the two of them made is the only place where the method is written down at length, sentence by sentence, in the years he was inventing it.
suggested_refs: Louise Colet, Lui: roman contemporain (1859)

stops.name: Paris, the Revue de Paris serialization
stops.date_confidence: attested: 1 October to 15 December 1856
stops.campa: Du Camp, now editing the Revue de Paris, runs the novel in instalments from the first of October to the fifteenth of December, cutting as he goes and cutting badly. Flaubert protests, has a disclaimer printed, and watches his sentences appear with the rhythm knocked out of them. The magazine is already under the eye of the imperial prosecutors for its politics. A book about a bored adulteress in Normandy is the pretext they have been waiting for, and the cab scene in the sixth instalment supplies it exactly.
suggested_refs: The Revue de Paris instalments, October to December 1856

stops.name: Palais de Justice, Paris, the acquittal
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Flaubert, the printer, and the publisher stand trial for outrage to public morals and to religion. The prosecutor Pinard reads the cab scene and the extreme unction aloud to the court as the evidence against them. On the seventh of February the tribunal acquits, with a reprimand attached. Two months later Michel Levy Freres publish in two volumes and the book sells on the scandal, the prosecution having done more for its sales than any review could.
stops.quote: Axiom: Hatred of the bourgeois is the beginning of virtue. But I include in the word bourgeois, the bourgeois in blouses as well the bourgeois in coats.
stops.quote_source: The George Sand-Gustave Flaubert Letters, Letter LVII, Flaubert to Sand, Paris, Friday morning, Project Gutenberg ebook #5115
suggested_refs: The requisitoire of the imperial prosecutor Ernest Pinard, January 1857

stops.name: Croisset, Salammbo begun
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia FR chronology)
stops.campa: Five months after the acquittal he starts the opposite book: Carthage in the third century before Christ, mercenaries in revolt, a priestess, elephants, a language of purple and iron. He reads more than a hundred volumes of ancient history before writing a line. Having been prosecuted for describing a Norman market town too exactly, he goes as far from Normandy as the record allows and applies to a dead city the rule he applied to Yonville, which is that nothing goes on the page that cannot be documented from somewhere.
suggested_refs: Flaubert's Carthage reading notes, 1857-1862

stops.name: Medina of Tunis, the landing
stops.date_confidence: attested: the research trip runs 12 April to 5 June 1858
stops.campa: He sails from Marseille and lands in Tunisia on the twelfth of April, staying until the fifth of June. He walks the medina, rides out into the countryside, takes down the light and the dust and the colour of the soil, and buys books. It is the only research trip he makes for a novel already begun and half written. He comes home and throws out most of the draft, having discovered that the Carthage in his head does not match the ground, and rewrites the book against the ground.
suggested_refs: The Tunisian notebooks of April to June 1858

stops.name: Byrsa Hill, Carthage, nothing standing
stops.date_confidence: within the attested April-June 1858 trip; month and day placed by inference
stops.campa: On Byrsa, the acropolis of the city Rome erased, he finds almost nothing: foundations, cisterns, potsherds, a hill with a view of the gulf. The Punic city is not there to be looked at. He writes home that the ruins are worthless and that he will have to build the whole thing out of texts and imagination after all. That is what he does, and the result is a novel so heavily armoured with sources that scholars spend the next century arguing with its footnotes instead of its sentences.
sources: Flaubert's 1858 letters on the scarcity of Carthaginian remains
suggested_refs: The Byrsa excavations and the state of Punic Carthage in 1858

stops.name: Paris, Salammbo published
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted to 01. The publication falls late in 1862, but no reachable source in this pass fixes the day
stops.campa: The book appears in 1862 and sells at once. Paris takes up Punic fashions, the archaeologists attack the accuracy, Sainte-Beuve attacks the taste, and Flaubert answers both at length and in public, which he never does again. George Sand defends it in print. He writes to thank her, and out of that letter grows the friendship and the correspondence of his last eighteen years, conducted between an old republican who believes in people and a hermit at Croisset who does not and says so in every third paragraph.
stops.quote_source: The George Sand-Gustave Flaubert Letters, Letter I, Flaubert to Sand, 1863, Project Gutenberg ebook #5115 (emphasis in the original translation)
suggested_refs: Sainte-Beuve's three Salammbo articles and Flaubert's published reply, 1862

stops.name: Croisset, L'Education sentimentale
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the start, 1 September 1864; the completion on 16 May 1869 is likewise attested
stops.campa: On the first of September he begins the book he has been circling since he was twenty: Paris in the 1840s, the revolution of 1848 seen from the pavement, and a young man in love with an older woman he never has. Elisa Schlesinger from the Trouville sand becomes Madame Arnoux. He works four years and eight months and finishes on the sixteenth of May 1869. It is the most deliberately anticlimactic novel of the century, a history of a generation written as a record of the things that did not happen to it.
stops.quote: I think that the artist should not manifest anything of his own feelings, and that the artist should not appear any more in his work than God in nature. The man is nothing, the work is everything!
stops.quote_source: The George Sand-Gustave Flaubert Letters, Letter CCCI, Flaubert to Sand, December 1875, Project Gutenberg ebook #5115
suggested_refs: The L'Education sentimentale manuscript scenarios, 1863-1869

stops.name: Paris, L'Education sentimentale published to a cold room
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Levy publishes in November and the reception runs from reserved to hostile. Readers who wanted another Bovary get a book in which nothing culminates and the hero fails at everything without even the dignity of a catastrophe. Four months earlier Louis Bouilhet died, the friend who had read every page of everything for twenty-five years. Sainte-Beuve dies the same autumn. Flaubert is forty-seven, and the room he has been writing into is emptying: the reviewers cold, the readers puzzled, the one ear he trusted gone.
stops.quote: Nervous analysis of the smallest facts, a notation of life that is both meticulous and alive.
stops.quote_source: Emile Zola on Flaubert, La Tribune, 28 November 1869; cited via Wikiquote, not independently verified in the original Zola text
suggested_refs: The 1869 reviews of L'Education sentimentale

stops.name: Croisset, the Prussians in the house
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the occupation of Croisset and the refuge at Rouen; month inferred from the campaign, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The war goes badly and the Prussians come down the Seine. Flaubert buries his papers, drills briefly with a National Guard company he despises, and abandons Croisset; a detachment quarters itself in the house through the winter, sleeping in the rooms where Bovary was written. He takes refuge in Rouen with his mother and his niece Caroline. The Commune follows in the spring and he watches Paris burn at a distance, writing to Sand that the whole century has been a fraud and that he would like to be somewhere else entirely.
stops.quote: I cherish the following dream: of going to live in the sun in a tranquil country.
stops.quote_source: Flaubert to George Sand, quoted in the editor's introduction to The George Sand-Gustave Flaubert Letters, Project Gutenberg ebook #5115, in connection with his reaction to the Paris Commune
suggested_refs: The Prussian occupation of the Croisset house, winter 1870-1871

stops.name: Croisset, the mother dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: His mother dies on the sixth of April and he is alone in the long house for the first time in fifty years. Within two years he ruins himself outright to save his niece's husband from bankruptcy, signing away the income that let him write without selling, and ends his life on a pension arranged by friends and a sinecure he never has to attend. He does not stop working. Bouvard et Pecuchet, the encyclopedia of human stupidity, is begun in this emptied house and is not finished in it.
stops.quote: Why are you so sad? Humanity offers nothing new. Its irremediable misery has filled me with sadness ever since my youth.
stops.quote_source: Flaubert to George Sand, quoted in the editor's introduction to The George Sand-Gustave Flaubert Letters, Project Gutenberg ebook #5115
suggested_refs: The Commanville bankruptcy and Flaubert's 1875 ruin

stops.name: Paris, the last Temptation of Saint Anthony
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted to 01. Essay 196 of the corpus dates a first publication of the Temptation to 1849, which is the year of the first manuscript version; the two dates are left standing side by side
stops.campa: Twenty-five years after Bouilhet told him to burn it, he publishes the third and final Tentation de saint Antoine. The hermit sits before his cave in the Thebaid and the night brings him everything: heresiarchs, the Queen of Sheba, Nebuchadnezzar on all fours eating grass, Vishnu, the dog-headed Anubis, the whole catalogue of gods reduced to a procession across one man's insomnia. The same insomnia gives Saint Christopher his dog's head in one passage, a detail borrowed straight from the legend rather than invented. Flaubert puts them all in one desert, twenty-five years of reading compressed into a single night.
stops.quote: The sense of the grotesque has restrained me from an inclination towards a disorderly life.
stops.quote_source: The George Sand-Gustave Flaubert Letters, Letter XVII, Flaubert to Sand, Croisset, 1866, Project Gutenberg ebook #5115
suggested_refs: La Tentation de saint Antoine, Charpentier, 1874
Essay 180 on the hermit's procession of gods

stops.name: Paris, Trois Contes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia FR chronology)
stops.campa: Three stories published together on the twenty-fourth of April: a Norman servant who loves a parrot, a medieval saint who kills every animal he meets and then carries a leper across a river, and the beheading of John the Baptist in Herod's fortress. Modern, medieval, ancient; Normandy, the stained glass of Rouen cathedral, the Judaea he crossed in 1850. It is the most admired thing he ever writes and the shortest, made in a year of financial ruin as a rest from the encyclopedia of stupidity that will not come right.
suggested_refs: The Saint Julian window in Rouen cathedral, source of La Legende de saint Julien l'Hospitalier

stops.name: Croisset, the sudden hemorrhage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The frequently repeated detail that he died at his writing desk is not supported by any source consulted and is not asserted here
stops.campa: He dies at Croisset on the eighth of May, apparently of a cerebral hemorrhage, at fifty-eight. The often repeated detail that he was found at his writing desk is not in the sources; the French account gives only a sudden hemorrhage in the house, and the 1911 Britannica only a stroke of apoplexy. Bouvard et Pecuchet stops mid-book, its second volume surviving as notes for a Dictionary of Received Ideas. Zola, Maupassant, Daudet, and Goncourt come up from Paris, and the man Maupassant called his master is buried three days later.
suggested_refs: The unfinished manuscript of Bouvard et Pecuchet and the Dictionnaire des idees recues

stops.name: Cimetiere monumental de Rouen, the family vault
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinate reconciled to the cemetery's own position given by Wikipedia FR; all three research lenses supplied different and wrong pins for it
stops.campa: He goes into the family vault on the hill above Rouen, a mile and a half from the hospital apartment where he was born. Rouen tells the story that the coffin would not fit the plot and the gravediggers had to improvise at the edge, which is either true or the kind of thing his own novels would have arranged. The house at Croisset is pulled down soon after and only the garden pavilion survives, listed as a monument historique in 1914, holding his inkstand and the gilded Buddha off his desk. Some three hundred and ten French streets carry his name.
